extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, policymakers, and stakeholders interested in U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: A concise overview of U.S. patentability, prosecution, enforcement, and policy issues that summarizes statutory requirements ( §§101,102,103,112), procedural forums (USPTO, PTAB, federal courts, ITC), and emerging topics such as Bayh-Dole march-in rights and AI-related inventorship questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-Eligible Subject Matter (Section 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 of the Patent Act allows patents on any process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. The statutory scope of patent-eligible subject matter is broad but federal courts have long held that laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas may not be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have developed judicially created exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). A series of Supreme Court decisions in the 2010s established the Alice/Mayo framework, which narrowed patent eligibility and affected fields such as computer software, business methods, and biotechnology. Stakeholders disagree about whether those decisions increase uncertainty or foster innovation by preventing monopolies on basic research tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility Requirement (Section 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 also requires an invention to be useful to be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard for the utility requirement is low, requiring only that the claimed invention have some benefit to the public that is not so vague as to be meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (35 U.S.C. §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must be novel (i.e., new). Under 35 U.S.C. §102, USPTO does not issue a patent if it finds that the claimed invention was already disclosed in the prior art (e.g., an earlier patent, product, or publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art includes earlier patents, publications, products, public use, or offers/sales before the patent application was filed. USPTO therefore denies a patent if the claimed invention had already been patented, publicly described, publicly used, or on sale before the patent application was filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claimed invention is novel, the invention must also be nonobvious to be patentable under 35 U.S.C. §103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO and courts consider many factors from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field. An invention may be obvious if it differs only slightly from prior inventions or merely combines known elements in a predictable way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and Disclosure Requirements (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must enable the invention by describing it with enough detail to teach a person of ordinary skill in the field how to make and use it. The application’s claims must be sufficiently definite (clear and well-defined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enablement requirement ensures that the public can use the patented technology after the patent expires. Definiteness of claims informs others what is covered by the patent and what is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification, Drawings, and Claim Drafting (Application Content)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a patent, an inventor must file a patent application with USPTO that describes the claimed invention in detail through words and drawings in a written specification and proposes written patent claims which define the legal scope of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claims define the patent holder’s legal rights; clear drafting and sufficient disclosure are essential to prosecution and later enforcement. During prosecution, a patent examiner determines whether the application and claimed invention meet the legal requirements for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Prosecution / Examination Process
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application process is called patent examination or patent prosecution; USPTO examiners determine whether applications and claimed inventions meet legal requirements for patentability, and if so USPTO issues the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution involves back-and-forth interactions with examiners; the document notes USPTO received nearly 600,000 utility applications and issued over 300,000 patents in FY2023. Examination timing affects effective patent term and may give rise to term adjustment or extension claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Term and Term Extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid U.S. patent gives the patent holder a temporary monopoly; a patent’s term begins on the date that the patent application is granted and ends 20 years after the date that the underlying patent application was filed with USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patent examination typically takes a little more than 2 years, an average effective patent term is about 17 or 18 years. The Patent Act allows for extensions of a patent’s term based on delays in patent examination or in obtaining regulatory approval for patented drugs and medical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership, Assignment, and Licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership of a patent initially vests with the inventor or inventors; patents may be transferred or assigned to others and may be licensed to permit others to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment contracts often require employees to assign patent rights in inventions created while on the job to their employer. A licensee may pay lump sums or continuing royalties to the patent holder. In federally funded inventions the agency receives a license to use the invention for government purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Enforcement, Remedies, and Defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are not self-enforcing; to obtain relief for infringement, the patent holder must generally sue alleged infringers in federal court. The ITC can conduct proceedings that bar infringing goods from importation. Appeals go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons accused of infringement may defend by arguing noninfringement (their activities fall outside the claims), invalidity (the patent does not meet legal requirements), or unenforceability (e.g., inequitable conduct or fraud on USPTO).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB and Inter Partes Review (IPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) hears challenges to already-issued patents through administrative procedures such as inter partes review (IPR). Any person other than the patent holder can petition PTAB to review the validity of an already-issued patent based on lack of novelty or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If PTAB agrees with the petitioner, USPTO cancels the invalid patent claims. IPR is described as making it easier, faster, and less expensive to challenge a patent’s validity compared with making the same arguments in court. Critics argue IPR creates uncertainty and is unfair to patent holders; defenders say it improves patent quality and works as Congress intended. Some Members and stakeholders have proposed reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federally Funded Inventions and Bayh‑Dole / March‑In Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Bayh-Dole Act (P.L. 96-517), federal contractors or grantees generally retain the patent rights on inventions made with federal support while granting the federal funding agency a license to use the patented invention for government purposes without paying a royalty; the agency also retains authority to grant compulsory licenses known as march-in rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No federal agency has exercised march-in rights to date. Some stakeholders argue agencies should use march-in to lower prices on patented inventions (e.g., prescription drugs) made with federal support; others argue using march-in to lower prices conflicts with the statute and would harm innovation. Recent NIST draft guidance would advise agencies to consider price as a factor in some cases when deciding whether to exercise march-in rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and Artificial Intelligence (Inventorship & Eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI developments raise novel patent law questions: limitations on patent-eligible subject matter may prevent certain AI innovations from being patented if they seek to claim an abstract idea; inventorship for inventions created in whole or in part by AI raises questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has held that an invention made 'autonomously' by AI alone is not patentable because it lacks any human inventor. USPTO guidance indicates inventions made by humans using AI assistance may be patentable depending on the significance of the human contribution to the invention.
